system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2122-02-05 23:40:00 to 2122-02-09 19:10:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with alcoholic cirrhosis, hepatitis C, and a history of hepatocellular carcinoma treated with TACE and RFA, was admitted for rectal bleeding and right upper quadrant pain. He presented with bright red blood per rectum followed by black, watery stools and a drop in hemoglobin. Evaluation showed stable cirrhosis without decompensation, no active bleeding on endoscopy, and aphthous ulcers in the rectum and descending colon on colonoscopy, which were likely the source of bleeding. The bleeding resolved during admission, and he remained hemodynamically stable. He was discharged home with a short course of ciprofloxacin, continuation of all home medications, and plans to follow up with his primary care provider and transplant team for biopsy results and further evaluation of possible inflammatory bowel disease.
problems: Unspecified gastritis and gastroduodenitis, without mention of hemorrhage
Chronic hepatitis C without mention of hepatic coma
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of liver

TECHNIQUE:  Multiplanar T1- and T2-weighted images were acquired on a 1.5
Tesla magnet, including dynamic 3D imaging, obtained prior to, during, and
after the uneventful intravenous administration of 0.1 mmol/kg (9 mL of
Gadavist).  1 mg of intramuscular glucagon was also administered.  900 mL of
Volumen oral contrast was ingested, as per MR enterography protocol.

COMPARISON STUDIES:  MR of the abdomen, liver protocol, dated ___ MRI dated ___ and CT of the abdomen and pelvis dated ___.

FINDINGS:

There is no evidence of abnormal dilatation of small bowel loops.  No evidence
of stricture.  There is no evidence of mucosal or submucosal enhancement.  The
jejunal loops are located in the right upper quadrant while the ileal loops
are located in the left aspect of the abdomen.  The duodenum is seen
traversing the midline; however, it immediately transits into the right upper
quadrant without reaching the ligament of Treitz.  The superior mesenteric
artery is located immediately posterior to the superior mesenteric vein. 
These findings indicate malrotation without evidence of obstruction.  The
cecum and the residual colonic loops of bowel are normal in appearance and in
normal location.  

There is again seen a cirrhotic morphology of the liver and evidence of portal
hypertension with portosystemic varices.  The main portal vein is patent.
There is an intrinsically T1 hyperintense peripheral nodule in the lateral
segment of the left lobe of the liver (image 40, series 8) without evidence of
enhancement, stable from the prior study.  Again seen are segment VI/VII
post-TACE changes.
 There is again seen a replaced right hepatic artery which originates from the
superior mesenteric artery and replaced left hepatic artery which originates
from the left gastric artery.  There is a small left-sided retroperitoneal
cystic structure, likely a lymphangioma, which demonstrates T2 hyperintense
signal without enhancement.  There is no evidence of ascites.  Spleen is
enlarged, measuring 14 cm, stable from the prior studies.  

The osseous structures demonstrate multilevel degenerative changes in the
lumbosacral spine without evidence of enhancing abnormal lesions or
destructive lesions.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Small bowel malrotation with jejunal loops located in the right upper
quadrant and ileal loops located in the left aspect of the abdomen and
superior mesenteric artery located immediately posterior to the superior
mesenteric vein.  There is no evidence of obstruction.

2.  No evidence of inflammatory bowel disease; no evidence of stricture, 
dilatation or abnormal enhancement pattern.

3.  Normal appearance of the colonic loops of bowels.

4.  Cirrhotic morphology and stigmata of portal hypertension.  There is no
ascites.  Stable splenomegaly.

5.  Post-TACE changes within the segment VI/VII of the liver.  Patent portal
vein.

diagnoses.long_title: Unspecified viral hepatitis C without hepatic coma
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of liver

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you came in with nausea, vomiting, and some blood in your vomit. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Doctor. I started feeling sick yesterday evening. I threw up three times—mostly food, but one time there was bright red blood, maybe a few tablespoons.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any pain in your belly? Diarrhea? Black or bloody stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, pain in the lower right side. No diarrhea. Last bowel movement was yesterday—normal brown stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You were just discharged two days ago for similar symptoms. We’ll need to check if anything has changed. We’ll run some labs and get imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be okay? This keeps happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring you closely. Your vitals are stable. We’ll figure this out together.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. Your labs from last night show your hemoglobin is 9.5, which is low but stable compared to your last admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I feel so tired?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. You also have iron deficiency anemia. We’re looking into possible causes. No active bleeding now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had those ulcers found last time. Could that be it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. But your recent EGD didn’t show varices or active bleeding. The blood in your vomit may have come from a small tear in the stomach from vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So not my liver veins?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not this time. Your liver function is stable. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your ultrasound back. No ascites, which is good. Your spleen is still enlarged, but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the pain? Any idea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. You’re scheduled for an MR enterography tomorrow to look at your small intestine more closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s that for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a detailed MRI of your bowel. Given your chronic pain and ulcers, we want to rule out blockages or inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, your MR enterography is back. There’s no blockage, but you have a condition called small bowel malrotation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Malrotation? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means your small intestine didn’t rotate normally when you were developing in the womb. The jejunum is on the right side, ileum on the left.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not usually. But it might explain your pain and nausea, especially with solid foods. It could cause intermittent issues with digestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I feel sick after eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We don’t see a blockage now, but it might happen off and on. We’ll recommend a soft or liquid diet for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can live with that if it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also start you on metoclopramide. It helps your stomach empty faster, which might reduce nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your celiac panel came back. Your tTG-IgA is elevated—43, which is high. Total IgA is also high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Celiac? Like gluten allergy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It suggests possible celiac disease, which can cause anemia and gut inflammation. But we can’t confirm without a biopsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I stop eating gluten?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. If you stop gluten now, the test results could be affected. We’ll discuss it with your transplant team as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your hemoglobin is stable at 9.0. White blood cell count is low—2.9—but we’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from my liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Cirrhosis can lower blood counts. The transplant team will check it at your next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still nauseous sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added ondansetron for breakthrough nausea. Keep on the soft diet and metoclopramide. You’re improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transplant team reviewed your case. They’ll call you to schedule a nutrition consult.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I need help with what to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They’ll guide you on a diet that works with your malrotation and possible celiac issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, you’re doing well. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on your soft or liquid diet. Take metoclopramide three times a day and ondansetron if you feel nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue all your home medications—omeprazole, spironolactone, lactulose, rifaximin, and ciprofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I see the transplant team?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll call you for an appointment next week. They’ll check your CBC and discuss the celiac testing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the malrotation? Will that ever need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Surgery is only if there’s a blockage. For now, diet and meds should help control symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if you have severe pain, vomiting, or black stools. Otherwise, see you soon in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your tTG-IgA came back positive. It supports possible celiac disease. The team will follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I might need a gluten-free diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but only after full evaluation. Don’t change your diet yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll wait for the call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Rest well and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye, Doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with alcoholic cirrhosis, hepatitis C, and a history of hepatocellular carcinoma treated with TACE and RFA, was readmitted two days after discharge for recurrent abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and hematemesis. Evaluation revealed stable cirrhosis without decompensation, no active variceal bleeding, and a stable hemoglobin level. Imaging showed small bowel malrotation without obstruction, which may contribute to his chronic gastrointestinal symptoms. He was managed conservatively with a soft diet, metoclopramide for gastric motility, and ondansetron for nausea. Elevated tTG-IgA and total IgA levels suggest possible celiac disease, warranting outpatient evaluation. He remained hemodynamically stable, and his symptoms improved. He was discharged home with continued home medications, new prescriptions for metoclopramide and ondansetron, and follow-up plans with the transplant clinic for nutrition consultation, CBC monitoring, and further workup of celiac disease.
